nameStory: The "train wrecker" gets its dramatic name from its habit of growing on railroad ties and wooden railway infrastructure. This tough fungus can literally help break down the treated wood that holds train tracks in place, earning it a reputation as a force to be reckoned with in the railway world.
description: The Trainwrecker is a sturdy, cream-colored to pale brown mushroom with a scaly, rough-textured cap that looks like it's covered in tiny scales or patches. It typically grows 2-6 inches across with thick, white gills that have jagged, saw-like edges - hence another common name, "scaly sawgill." This is a wood-loving fungus that appears alone or in small clusters on dead or dying wood. The whole mushroom has a robust, almost leathery feel that matches its tough-guy reputation.

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: White to cream gills with distinctively jagged, saw-tooth edges that feel rough when you gently run your finger along them - like tiny serrated knives

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Cream to tan colored with dark brown scales scattered across the surface, feeling dry and slightly rough to the touch like fine sandpaper

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Thick, solid, and often off-center, colored similar to the cap with a tough, fibrous texture that's difficult to break by hand

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Pleasant, sweet anise or licorice-like fragrance that becomes more noticeable when the mushroom is crushed or cut

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: White spore print, obtained by placing the cap gill-side down on dark paper overnight

habitat: Look for Trainwreckers on dead hardwood logs, stumps, and wooden structures throughout New England's forests and even in suburban areas. They particularly favor oak, maple, and other deciduous wood, often appearing on old railroad ties, fence posts, and construction lumber. You'll find them from lowland forests up to moderate elevations, especially in areas where dead wood is abundant.

seasonality.spring: Early fruiting may begin as temperatures warm and spring rains provide moisture, though not yet at peak season.
seasonality.summer: Prime fruiting season with regular appearance after summer rains, when warm temperatures and moisture combine perfectly for growth.
seasonality.fall: Continued fruiting through early fall, especially after autumn rains, before cold weather slows growth.
seasonality.winter: Rarely active, though old specimens may persist as dried, leathery remnants on wood substrates.

funFact: This mushroom can actually digest the toxic preservatives in treated lumber, including creosote used on railroad ties - it's one of the few organisms tough enough to break down these harsh chemicals that are designed to prevent decay!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with oyster mushrooms, but the Trainwrecker's jagged gill edges are the dead giveaway - oyster mushrooms have smooth gill edges. Remember: "Trainwrecker tears, oysters are smooth."
contextualKnowledge: This species was recently moved from the genus Lentinus to Neolentinus based on DNA analysis, so you may see it listed under its old scientific name Lentinus lepideus in older field guides. The name change doesn't affect identification, but it shows how modern science keeps updating our understanding of fungal relationships.
compareHints: Since Trainwrecker is the only Neolentinus species commonly found in New England, compare it with other wood-decay fungi like oyster mushrooms and honey mushrooms. Unlike oyster mushrooms which have smooth gill edges and grow in overlapping clusters, Trainwrecker has those distinctive serrated gills and grows more individually. Honey mushrooms are smaller, darker, and grow in dense clusters with thin stems.
